title: BLS & ACLS Written Exam
blurb: The AHA BLS provider written test covers 25 items and the ACLS provider written test covers 50 items, both requiring 84% to pass; this practice attempt draws 50 questions pooled across both exams to mirror the mix you'll see in a real course.

questions.q: You are alone and find an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally. After confirming the scene is safe and calling for help/AED, what compression rate should you use for adult CPR?
choices: 100 to 120 compressions per minute
60 to 80 compressions per minute
At least 140 compressions per minute
80 to 100 compressions per minute
questions.why: AHA guidelines set the adult compression rate at 100-120/min; slower rates under-perfuse, and rates above 120/min reduce chest recoil and stroke volume, actually lowering coronary perfusion pressure.

questions.q: What is the correct adult chest compression depth during CPR?
choices: At least 1 inch
At least 2 inches but no more than 2.4 inches
At least 3 inches
1 to 1.5 inches
questions.why: 2-2.4 inches generates adequate intrathoracic pressure to circulate blood; shallower compressions under-perfuse the brain and heart, and depths beyond 2.4 inches raise injury risk without added benefit.

questions.q: A single rescuer is performing adult CPR without an advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used?
choices: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
30 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 1 breath
questions.why: 30:2 is the standard single-rescuer adult ratio. 15:2 is reserved for two-rescuer pediatric/infant CPR, not adults, so it is wrong here.

questions.q: Two trained rescuers are performing CPR on a 6-year-old with no advanced airway placed. What compression-to-ventilation ratio applies?
choices: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
10 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 2 breaths
questions.why: Two-rescuer pediatric and infant CPR uses 15:2 to allow more frequent ventilation for the child's higher oxygen demand; 30:2 is the single-rescuer ratio, not the two-rescuer pediatric one.

questions.q: During ongoing adult CPR, how often should rescuers switch the compressor role?
choices: About every 2 minutes
Every 30 seconds
Every 10 minutes
Only when the compressor asks
questions.why: Compressor fatigue sets in within about 2 minutes and silently degrades depth and rate even when the rescuer feels fine, so a scheduled swap every 2 minutes (roughly every 5 cycles of 30:2) keeps compression quality high.

questions.q: What is the target chest recoil expectation between compressions during high-quality CPR?
choices: Lean slightly on the chest between compressions
Allow full chest recoil after each compression
Recoil is not important if rate is met
Recoil only matters with an advanced airway
questions.why: Full recoil lets the heart refill between compressions, restoring venous return; leaning on the chest (incomplete recoil) raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts preload, lowering coronary perfusion even at a correct rate.

questions.q: What is the maximum acceptable interruption in chest compressions during CPR, such as for a pulse check or rhythm analysis?
choices: 30 seconds
1 minute
10 seconds
There is no limit as long as a reason is given
questions.why: Coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure drop rapidly once compressions stop, so pauses are capped at about 10 seconds; longer pauses (like a full minute) let perfusion pressure collapse and must be rebuilt from scratch.

questions.q: An AED is applied to an unresponsive, pulseless adult and advises 'shock advised.' What is the correct next action?
choices: Start rescue breathing before shocking
Perform 2 minutes of compressions before shocking
Give the shock while continuing compressions
Ensure everyone is clear of the patient, then deliver the shock
questions.why: A shock must be delivered with no one touching the patient to avoid injury; compressions must stop for the actual shock delivery, and breathing first would waste the narrow window when a shockable rhythm is confirmed.

questions.q: Immediately after an AED delivers a shock, what should rescuers do?
choices: Resume chest compressions immediately, starting with compressions
Check for a pulse before doing anything else
Wait for the AED to reanalyze before touching the patient
Give 2 rescue breaths first
questions.why: Post-shock myocardial stunning means a perfusing rhythm rarely returns instantly, so compressions resume right away; pausing to check a pulse or wait wastes perfusion time the heart needs.

questions.q: You find an adult who is unresponsive with occasional gasping breaths. How should you interpret this breathing pattern?
choices: This is normal breathing, so CPR is not needed yet
This is agonal gasping and counts as 'not breathing normally' — start CPR
Wait 2 more minutes to see if breathing improves
This means the airway is only partially obstructed, use back blows
questions.why: Agonal gasps are a common early sign of cardiac arrest, not effective breathing, so CPR must start immediately; waiting or treating it as normal breathing delays compressions during the highest-yield window.

questions.q: Where should hand placement be for adult chest compressions?
choices: Over the xiphoid process
On the left side of the chest over the apex
Center of the chest, on the lower half of the sternum
Upper third of the sternum near the clavicles
questions.why: The lower half of the sternum overlies the ventricles and maximizes stroke volume; pressing on the xiphoid risks lacerating the liver, and the upper sternum or lateral chest doesn't compress the heart effectively.

questions.q: A lone rescuer is performing infant CPR. What compression-to-ventilation ratio and landmark are correct?
choices: 15:2 using the heel of one hand on the sternum
30:2 using the heel of both hands
15:2 using two thumbs encircling the chest
30:2 using two fingers just below the nipple line
questions.why: A single rescuer uses 30:2 with two fingers just below the nipple line; the two-thumb encircling technique and 15:2 ratio are reserved for two-rescuer infant CPR, not a lone rescuer.

questions.q: Two rescuers are performing infant CPR. What compression technique is preferred?
choices: Two-thumb encircling-hands technique with 15:2
Two-finger technique with 30:2
One-hand heel technique with 15:2
Two-thumb technique with 30:2
questions.why: With two providers, the two-thumb encircling technique generates better depth and coronary perfusion than two fingers, paired with the two-rescuer 15:2 ratio; 30:2 is the single-rescuer ratio.

questions.q: For adult CPR with an advanced airway (such as an endotracheal tube) in place, how should ventilations and compressions be delivered?
choices: Pause compressions for every breath at a 30:2 ratio
Continuous compressions at 100-120/min with 1 breath every 6 seconds, asynchronously
Stop compressions every minute for 2 breaths
1 breath every 10 seconds with paused compressions
questions.why: Once an advanced airway is placed, compressions no longer pause for ventilation — they run continuously while one breath is delivered about every 6 seconds (10/min), asynchronous with compressions.

questions.q: What is the correct adult rescue breathing rate for a patient with a pulse who is not breathing adequately (respiratory arrest, no cardiac arrest)?
choices: 1 breath every 2 seconds
1 breath every 15 seconds
1 breath every 6 seconds (about 10/min)
1 breath every 30 seconds
questions.why: Adult rescue breathing without compressions is delivered at 1 breath every 6 seconds; slower rates under-ventilate, and every 2 seconds is far too fast and risks gastric insufflation.

questions.q: A conscious adult is choking and cannot cough, speak, or breathe. What is the first-line intervention?
choices: Back blows only, thrusts are never used
Finger sweep of the mouth immediately
Have the patient lie down and start CPR right away
Abdominal thrusts (or chest thrusts if pregnant/obese)
questions.why: For a conscious adult with complete airway obstruction, abdominal thrusts (or chest thrusts in pregnancy/obesity) are first-line; a blind finger sweep risks pushing the object deeper, and CPR is reserved for once the patient becomes unresponsive.

questions.q: A choking adult becomes unresponsive while you are performing abdominal thrusts. What should you do next?
choices: Start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, and check the mouth for a visible object before breaths
Continue abdominal thrusts while the patient is on the floor
Perform a blind finger sweep first, then compressions
Immediately call for a cricothyrotomy kit
questions.why: Once unresponsive, CPR replaces thrusts — compressions generate airway pressure that can dislodge the object — and rescuers only remove an object they can actually see, never a blind sweep.

questions.q: What is the correct technique for relieving choking in a responsive infant?
choices: Abdominal thrusts like an adult
Alternating 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts
Back blows only, no chest thrusts
Finger sweep of the mouth first
questions.why: Infants get 5 back blows alternated with 5 chest thrusts because abdominal thrusts risk organ injury in their soft, small abdomens; blind finger sweeps are avoided at any age.

questions.q: During two-rescuer adult CPR, what is the recommended way to communicate a change in the patient's rhythm or condition?
choices: Wait until the next pulse check to mention it
Write it down for the code record only
Say it out loud clearly to the team as it happens (closed-loop communication)
Only tell the team leader privately
questions.why: Closed-loop, out-loud communication ensures the whole team reacts in real time to changes like ROSC or a new rhythm; delaying the information to the next pulse check can cost critical seconds.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of high-quality chest compressions in cardiac arrest?
choices: To restart the heart's electrical activity directly
To warm the patient's core temperature
To clear the airway of secretions
To generate enough blood flow to deliver oxygen to the brain and heart
questions.why: Compressions are a mechanical pump substituting for the heart, perfusing the brain and coronary arteries; they do not themselves restart electrical activity — defibrillation and drugs address that.

questions.q: A rescuer is about to apply AED pads to a patient with a medication patch on the chest where a pad needs to go. What should be done?
choices: Remove the patch, wipe the area, and place the pad there
Place the pad directly over the patch
Skip that pad position entirely
Cover the patch with gauze and place the pad on top
questions.why: A transdermal patch can block energy delivery and cause skin burns, so it should be removed and the area wiped before pad placement; placing the pad on top or skipping the position risks ineffective defibrillation.

questions.q: An unresponsive adult is found in cardiac arrest and is lying face down in shallow water after a drowning. What is the correct BLS priority?
choices: Perform abdominal thrusts to clear water from the lungs first
Remove from water and begin CPR immediately, starting with rescue breaths if trained, then compressions
Wait for EMS before any intervention
Only start compressions once fully dried off
questions.why: Drowning arrest is primarily hypoxic, so early ventilation matters; abdominal thrusts to 'drain the lungs' are not effective and delay care, and CPR should not be delayed for full drying.

questions.q: What AED pad placement is used for an adult patient?
choices: Both pads on the left side of the chest only
One pad on the abdomen, one on the back
One pad on the upper right chest, one pad on the lower left side/ribs (anterolateral)
Both pads directly over the sternum
questions.why: Standard anterolateral placement (upper-right sternal border, lower-left ribs at the midaxillary line) puts the heart between the pads for effective current delivery; placing both pads on one side won't capture the heart in the current path.

questions.q: For a pediatric patient in cardiac arrest, when should pediatric AED pads/dose-attenuator be used instead of adult pads?
choices: Never — adult pads are used at every age
Only for infants under 6 months
For any patient under age 18
For children under about 8 years old or under 55 lb (25 kg) when available
questions.why: Pediatric attenuated pads reduce the delivered energy appropriately for smaller bodies and are used under about age 8 or 55 lb when available; if only adult pads exist, they are used rather than withholding defibrillation.

questions.q: If pediatric AED pads are not available for an infant in cardiac arrest, what should the rescuer do?
choices: Use adult pads/adult AED rather than withhold defibrillation
Do not defibrillate an infant under any circumstance
Cut an adult pad in half and use only that piece
Wait for pediatric pads to arrive before shocking
questions.why: Some defibrillation is better than none — adult pads are used if pediatric ones aren't available; cutting a pad or withholding the shock entirely delays treatment of a shockable rhythm.

questions.q: A rescuer is unsure whether an unresponsive patient has a pulse after a 10-second check. What should they do?
choices: Keep checking the pulse for another full minute
Begin chest compressions
Assume a pulse is present and only give breaths
Wait for a second rescuer to confirm before acting
questions.why: If a pulse cannot be confidently felt within about 10 seconds, treat as pulseless and start compressions; delaying for further checks wastes time when the patient may be in arrest.

questions.q: What best describes 'chain of survival' for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
choices: Only calling 911 and waiting for paramedics
Compressions alone, without any other steps
Early recognition/activation, early CPR, early defibrillation, basic and advanced EMS care, post-arrest care, and recovery
Defibrillation first, before any other action
questions.why: The chain of survival links every stage from bystander recognition through post-arrest care and recovery — skipping straight to defibrillation without recognition, CPR, and activation breaks the chain and lowers survival.

questions.q: During CPR training, what is meant by 'minimizing interruptions' to compressions?
choices: Never stopping compressions for any reason, even shocks
Performing compressions only during the first 2 minutes
Interruptions do not matter if the rate is correct
Keeping the fraction of time compressions are actually happening (chest compression fraction) as high as possible, ideally above 60%
questions.why: Chest compression fraction — the percent of arrest time spent actually compressing — strongly predicts survival, so unnecessary pauses (beyond required ones like shock delivery) are minimized; a high compression rate does not offset a low compression fraction.

questions.q: A bystander without CPR training is coached by a 911 dispatcher during a witnessed adult collapse. What is the dispatcher likely to recommend?
choices: Hands-only (compression-only) CPR
Full CPR including rescue breaths, mandatory for any bystander
No action until EMS arrives
Only checking for a pulse repeatedly
questions.why: Hands-only CPR is recommended for untrained bystanders because it's simpler to coach by phone and still provides meaningful circulation in the first minutes; withholding all action lets perfusion stop completely.

questions.q: What is the correct action if an AED analyzes the rhythm and states 'no shock advised'?
choices: Remove the AED pads since no shock is needed
Immediately resume high-quality CPR starting with compressions
Stop all resuscitation efforts
Wait 2 minutes before touching the patient again
questions.why: 'No shock advised' means the rhythm is non-shockable (like PEA or asystole), which still requires ongoing CPR — it is not a stopping point; compressions resume right away rather than waiting.

questions.q: What effect does excessive ventilation (too fast or too large breaths) have during CPR?
choices: It has no effect on blood flow during CPR
It improves oxygen delivery with no downside
It raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return, lowering blood flow generated by compressions
It only matters if an advanced airway is in place
questions.why: Over-ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, impeding venous return to the heart and reducing the cardiac output that compressions are trying to generate — a real physiologic downside, not a neutral action.

questions.q: For a pregnant patient in cardiac arrest who is visibly term or near-term, what BLS modification is recommended?
choices: Compress the abdomen instead of the chest
Withhold defibrillation because of the fetus
Position the patient prone for compressions
Perform manual left uterine displacement while continuing standard compressions
questions.why: Left uterine displacement relieves aortocaval compression from the gravid uterus, improving venous return during standard chest compressions; defibrillation is still performed, and compressions remain on the chest, not the abdomen.

questions.q: A patient with a known opioid overdose is found unresponsive and not breathing, with a weak but present pulse. What is the correct BLS action?
choices: Give rescue breaths and administer naloxone if available, while preparing for CPR if the pulse is lost
Start chest compressions immediately since a pulse is present
Only give naloxone and nothing else
Wait for the patient to self-resolve since opioids ' wear off'
questions.why: With a pulse present, respiratory support (rescue breathing) and naloxone address the primary problem — respiratory depression; compressions are reserved for when the pulse is lost, not started on a perfusing patient.

questions.q: What is the correct recovery position use case in BLS?
choices: For a patient in cardiac arrest to allow easier compressions
For an unresponsive patient who is breathing normally and has a pulse, to protect the airway
For a choking patient instead of abdominal thrusts
For any patient during multi-casualty triage
questions.why: The recovery position keeps the airway clear of secretions/vomit in a breathing, pulseless-negative (has a pulse) unresponsive patient; a pulseless patient needs supine positioning for CPR, not the recovery position.

questions.q: When performing CPR on a hard surface versus a soft mattress, why does surface matter?
choices: Surface has no effect on compression effectiveness
A soft surface always improves recoil
A soft surface absorbs compression force, reducing effective depth delivered to the chest
Compressions should never be done on a firm surface
questions.why: A soft mattress compresses along with the chest, so less of the rescuer's force reaches the heart; moving the patient to the floor or using a backboard restores effective depth.

questions.q: What does 'push hard, push fast' in adult CPR correspond to numerically?
choices: At least 1 inch depth at a rate of 60/min
At least 3 inches depth at any rate
2 inches depth at exactly 80/min
At least 2 inches depth at a rate of 100-120/min
questions.why: This is the plain-language summary of the two most survival-linked compression metrics: adequate depth (2-2.4 in) and adequate rate (100-120/min); the distractors misstate one or both numbers.

questions.q: A rescuer is switching compressor roles during two-rescuer CPR. What is the best way to minimize the pause in compressions during the switch?
choices: Coordinate the switch to happen quickly, ideally in under 5 seconds, often timed with a rhythm check
Always take a full 30-second break during the switch
Switch only after 10 minutes of continuous compressions
There is no need to minimize the pause
questions.why: A fast, coordinated switch (often folded into a scheduled rhythm/pulse check) keeps the compression fraction high; a long deliberate break unnecessarily drops perfusion pressure.

questions.q: What is a key sign of effective CPR that rescuers or EMS may monitor with capnography?
choices: An ETCO2 reading of zero, which confirms good perfusion
An end-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) reading that rises and stays consistently above about 10-20 mmHg
Capnography cannot be used during CPR
A falling ETCO2 confirms compressions are working
questions.why: ETCO2 reflects pulmonary blood flow generated by compressions; a low or falling value suggests ineffective compressions or arrest, while a sustained value above roughly 10-20 mmHg indicates reasonable perfusion during CPR.

questions.q: A sudden, sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR (for example jumping from 15 to 45 mmHg) most likely indicates what?
choices: The airway has become obstructed
The patient has developed a tension pneumothorax
Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)
The monitor is malfunctioning and should be replaced
questions.why: A sudden ETCO2 surge reflects a jump in pulmonary blood flow, the hallmark of ROSC; obstruction or a pneumothorax would drop or flatten the waveform, not spike it.

questions.q: When should CPR be started for an unresponsive patient with no normal breathing and no definite pulse found within 10 seconds, regardless of setting (BLS, ED, or field)?
choices: Only after a monitor is attached to confirm the rhythm
Only after IV access is obtained
Only once a physician is present to order it
Immediately, without waiting for additional equipment
questions.why: CPR is a time-critical bystander/BLS skill that should never wait on monitoring, IV access, or a physician's presence — every second of delay lowers survival, and equipment/orders can be arranged during ongoing compressions.

questions.q: What is the correct hand position adjustment for adult CPR if the rescuer is much smaller or has limited strength?
choices: Use body weight with straight arms and shoulders directly over the hands, switching compressors more frequently if needed
Bend the elbows to push harder with the arm muscles
Compress more shallowly to conserve strength
Kneel to the side of the patient's head instead of the chest
questions.why: Straight arms with shoulders over the hands let body weight (not arm strength) generate depth, which works regardless of rescuer size; bending the elbows fatigues the rescuer faster and reduces consistent depth.

questions.q: What best describes the correct technique for delivering a rescue breath during CPR with a bag-mask device?
choices: Give the largest volume the bag can deliver
Give just enough volume to produce visible chest rise over about 1 second
Squeeze the bag as fast as possible regardless of chest rise
Deliver breaths over 3-4 seconds each for full lung filling
questions.why: A breath delivered over about 1 second with visible chest rise avoids gastric insufflation and over-ventilation; maximal volume or slow, prolonged breaths both risk complications without improving oxygenation.

questions.q: Why is early defibrillation emphasized so strongly in the BLS chain of survival for witnessed VF arrest?
choices: Defibrillation has no time sensitivity
CPR alone is equally effective as defibrillation for VF
Survival from VF drops roughly 7-10% for every minute defibrillation is delayed without CPR
Defibrillation only works after 10 minutes of CPR
questions.why: VF is time-sensitive — survival falls sharply with each passing minute without defibrillation; CPR buys time and supports perfusion but does not convert the rhythm the way a shock can.

questions.q: An AED user notices the patient has a wet chest (just pulled from a pool). What should be done before applying pads?
choices: Apply the pads directly to the wet skin
Do not use the AED at all if the chest is wet
Pour more water on the chest to improve conduction
Quickly dry the chest before placing the pads
questions.why: Water on the chest can shunt electrical current across the skin instead of through the heart and reduce shock effectiveness, so the chest is dried first; withholding the AED entirely is unnecessary once dried.

questions.q: What is the correct BLS approach for an unresponsive adult with a suspected spinal injury who needs CPR?
choices: Start CPR as normal; spinal precautions do not override the need for compressions/airway management
Withhold CPR entirely to avoid worsening a spinal injury
Only perform compressions, never open the airway
Wait for a backboard before starting any care
questions.why: An unresponsive, pulseless patient dies without CPR far sooner than a spinal injury would cause harm from careful handling — compressions and airway management proceed immediately, with in-line stabilization added as available, not withheld.

questions.q: During team-based BLS, what should the person managing the airway say to confirm they heard an instruction from the team leader?
choices: Nod silently and proceed
Repeat the instruction back before performing it (closed-loop communication)
Say 'okay' with no further detail
Wait for the leader to repeat it a second time
questions.why: Closed-loop communication — repeating the order back — confirms it was heard correctly and reduces errors; a silent nod or vague acknowledgment gives the leader no confirmation the right task was understood.

questions.q: What is the correct BLS response to an unresponsive patient who is breathing normally and has a pulse, found lying supine after a fall with no other information available?
choices: Begin chest compressions immediately as a precaution
Give rescue breaths every 6 seconds despite normal breathing
Maintain the airway, monitor breathing and pulse closely, and prepare to reposition (e.g., recovery position) if needed while awaiting further care
Perform abdominal thrusts to rule out choking
questions.why: A breathing patient with a pulse does not need compressions or rescue breathing — the priority is airway protection and monitoring; compressions on a perfusing, breathing patient can cause harm and are not indicated.

questions.q: What is the correct compression rate range if a metronome or feedback device is available during CPR?
choices: Set it to 60 beats per minute
Set it to 150 beats per minute
Feedback devices should not be used during CPR
Set it to 100-120 beats per minute to pace compressions
questions.why: Feedback/metronome devices are set within the guideline compression rate range (100-120/min) to help rescuers maintain consistent, effective compressions; slower or much faster settings would coach the rescuer into an incorrect rate.

questions.q: A single rescuer must leave a witnessed adult collapse briefly to retrieve an AED. What is the correct BLS sequence?
choices: Call for help/activate EMS, retrieve the AED if immediately available, then start CPR while it is applied
Never leave the patient for any reason, even to get an AED
Perform 10 minutes of CPR before considering an AED
Wait for someone else to arrive before doing anything
questions.why: For witnessed adult collapse, quickly getting the AED matters because early defibrillation drives survival; the rescuer activates EMS, grabs a nearby AED, and starts CPR, applying the AED as soon as it's available rather than delaying either action.

questions.q: A monitor shows ventricular fibrillation in a pulseless patient. What is the immediate next step after confirming pulselessness?
choices: Defibrillate as soon as possible
Give amiodarone 300 mg IV before any shock
Begin synchronized cardioversion
Administer atropine 1 mg IV
questions.why: VF is a shockable rhythm and defibrillation is the single most effective treatment; antiarrhythmics and atropine do not substitute for early defibrillation, and synchronized cardioversion is for organized rhythms, not VF.

questions.q: After the first defibrillation attempt for VF fails to convert the rhythm, what is the correct next step?
choices: Shock again immediately without resuming CPR
Resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes, then reassess the rhythm
Check a pulse before doing anything else
Switch immediately to synchronized cardioversion
questions.why: After any shock, CPR resumes right away for a full 2-minute cycle before the next rhythm/pulse check — myocardial stunning means a perfusing rhythm rarely returns instantly, so an immediate second shock or pulse check wastes perfusion time.

questions.q: When should epinephrine be given during a cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm (VF/pVT)?
choices: Before the first shock, always
Only after 20 minutes of resuscitation
After the second shock, then every 3-5 minutes
Never, epinephrine is only for non-shockable rhythms
questions.why: For shockable rhythms, epinephrine is typically started after the second defibrillation attempt (once CPR/shocks have had a first chance to work) and then repeated every 3-5 minutes; it is not withheld from shockable rhythms.

questions.q: What is the standard adult IV/IO epinephrine dose during cardiac arrest?
choices: 0.1 mg every minute
10 mg once, then stop
1 mg once only, no repeat dosing
1 mg every 3-5 minutes
questions.why: 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes is the standard adult arrest dose; 0.1 mg is a pediatric-scale amount and 10 mg is a gross overdose, and arrest dosing is repeated, not a single dose.

questions.q: A patient remains in refractory VF after 3 shocks and epinephrine. What antiarrhythmic and dose is given first?
choices: Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO
Amiodarone 150 mg IV/IO as the first dose
Lidocaine 300 mg IV/IO
Adenosine 6 mg IV/IO
questions.why: The first amiodarone dose in refractory VF/pVT is 300 mg IV/IO; 150 mg is the second dose if VF persists, lidocaine has a different dosing scheme, and adenosine is not used in shockable-rhythm arrest.

questions.q: If VF/pVT persists after the first dose of amiodarone, what is the second dose?
choices: 300 mg IV/IO again
150 mg IV/IO
75 mg IV/IO
600 mg IV/IO
questions.why: The amiodarone regimen is 300 mg first dose, then 150 mg for a second dose if the shockable rhythm persists; repeating the full 300 mg or doubling to 600 mg is not the guideline-based regimen.

questions.q: A team chooses lidocaine instead of amiodarone for refractory VF. What is the correct initial dose?
choices: 0.1 to 0.15 mg/kg IV/IO
5 to 7.5 mg/kg IV/IO
1 to 1.5 mg/kg IV/IO
150 mg/kg IV/IO
questions.why: Lidocaine's initial arrest dose is 1-1.5 mg/kg IV/IO; the other values are either a tenth of the correct dose or wildly excessive relative to weight-based dosing.

questions.q: If lidocaine is redosed for persistent VF/pVT, what is the follow-up dose?
choices: 1 to 1.5 mg/kg IV/IO again, unchanged
3 mg/kg IV/IO
0.05 mg/kg IV/IO
0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg IV/IO
questions.why: The lidocaine redose is a smaller 0.5-0.75 mg/kg dose, not a repeat of the full initial dose; 3 mg/kg exceeds the typical total dose ceiling and 0.05 mg/kg is far too low to have an effect.

questions.q: A cardiac monitor shows a rhythm with no discernible QRS complexes and a pulseless patient. What rhythm category is this and what is the treatment approach?
choices: Asystole — a non-shockable rhythm treated with CPR and epinephrine, no defibrillation
A shockable rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation
Synchronized cardioversion is indicated
Adenosine should be given first
questions.why: Asystole has no organized or fibrillating electrical activity to shock, so defibrillation does nothing; management is high-quality CPR plus epinephrine and a search for reversible causes, not a shock.

questions.q: A patient is pulseless but the monitor shows an organized rhythm with a normal-appearing QRS complex. What is this called and how is it managed?
choices: Ventricular fibrillation, shock immediately
Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) — treated with CPR, epinephrine, and identifying/treating reversible causes
This is a normal perfusing rhythm, no treatment needed
Synchronized cardioversion should be performed
questions.why: PEA is organized electrical activity without a palpable pulse; because there's no fibrillation or pulseless VT to shock, treatment centers on CPR, epinephrine, and correcting a reversible H or T cause, not defibrillation.

questions.q: When should epinephrine be given during cardiac arrest with a non-shockable rhythm (PEA/asystole)?
choices: Only after 3 failed defibrillation attempts
Never — epinephrine is only for shockable rhythms
As soon as feasible after the rhythm is identified, then every 3-5 minutes
After 20 minutes if no other drug has worked
questions.why: For non-shockable rhythms, epinephrine is given as early as possible (unlike the shockable pathway, which delays it until after the second shock) and then every 3-5 minutes; defibrillation attempts are irrelevant since the rhythm isn't shockable.

questions.q: What does the mnemonic 'H's and T's' in cardiac arrest refer to?
choices: The order in which defibrillation shocks are delivered
A checklist for post-arrest hospital discharge
The steps of synchronized cardioversion
A list of reversible causes of arrest to actively search for and treat
questions.why: H's and T's is a systematic memory aid for reversible causes of PEA/asystole (and refractory VF) — hypovolemia through thrombosis — prompting the team to look beyond just 'more epi, more CPR' for a fixable underlying problem.

questions.q: Name the correct set of 'H's' in the H's and T's mnemonic for reversible cardiac arrest causes.
choices: Hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo/hyperkalemia, hypothermia
Hypertension, hyperglycemia, hemorrhage, headache, hepatitis
Hypoxia, hypertension, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, hemolysis
Hyperkalemia, hypertension, hydration, hypoxia, hemothorax
questions.why: The correct five H's are hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo/hyperkalemia, and hypothermia; the distractors substitute conditions (like hypertension or hyperglycemia) that are not part of the standard mnemonic.

questions.q: Name the correct set of 'T's' in the H's and T's mnemonic for reversible cardiac arrest causes.
choices: Trauma, tachycardia, tremor, thyroid storm, transfusion reaction
Tension pneumothorax, tamponade (cardiac), toxins, thrombosis (pulmonary), thrombosis (coronary)
Tension headache, tamponade, toxins, tachypnea, thrombosis
Thrombosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, tetanus, trauma
questions.why: The correct five T's are tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, and coronary thrombosis; distractors substitute non-standard items like tachycardia, thyroid storm, or tetanus.

questions.q: A patient in PEA arrest has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation. Which H or T is most likely?
choices: Hypovolemia
Hypothermia
Tension pneumothorax
Toxins
questions.why: Distended neck veins with unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation are classic for tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock; hypovolemia typically causes flat neck veins, not distended ones, and the other options don't explain this exam picture.

questions.q: A patient in PEA arrest has a history of recent central line placement and muffled heart sounds with distended neck veins. Which reversible cause is most likely?
choices: Hypoxia
Hypokalemia
Pulmonary thrombosis
Cardiac tamponade
questions.why: Muffled heart sounds plus distended neck veins after a central line procedure suggests tamponade from vessel/cardiac perforation; the other choices don't fit this specific triad of findings tied to a recent invasive procedure.

questions.q: A dialysis patient goes into cardiac arrest with peaked T waves noted on the monitor before arrest. Which H or T should be treated urgently?
choices: Hyperkalemia
Hypothermia
Tension pneumothorax
Thrombosis, coronary
questions.why: Peaked T waves in a dialysis patient point strongly to hyperkalemia as the arrest trigger, treated with calcium chloride, insulin/glucose, and bicarbonate; the other options don't have a specific ECG or dialysis-history link like this.

questions.q: During a resuscitation, what is the recommended maximum interval between rhythm/pulse checks?
choices: Every 30 seconds
About every 2 minutes (5 cycles of CPR)
Every 10 minutes
Only at the very end of the code
questions.why: Rhythm and pulse checks occur roughly every 2 minutes to balance getting timely information against interrupting compressions too often; checking every 30 seconds would interrupt CPR excessively, and every 10 minutes is far too infrequent.

questions.q: What airway strategy is generally preferred during the earliest minutes of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation?
choices: Immediate endotracheal intubation before any compressions
Cricothyrotomy as the first airway step
Bag-mask ventilation with good technique, delaying advanced airway placement if it would interrupt compressions
No ventilation at all until ROSC
questions.why: Early, well-performed bag-mask ventilation with minimal compression interruption is prioritized over rushing intubation, which can cause a costly pause; cricothyrotomy is a rescue airway, not a first-line arrest step, and ventilation is still needed during arrest.

questions.q: What is the purpose of using waveform capnography during cardiac arrest management?
choices: To measure blood glucose during the code
To replace the need for a defibrillator
To determine the patient's core temperature
To confirm airway placement and monitor CPR quality/detect ROSC via ETCO2 trends
questions.why: Capnography confirms correct advanced airway placement and its ETCO2 trend reflects perfusion from compressions, helping detect ROSC; it has no role in glucose or temperature monitoring and does not replace defibrillation.

questions.q: A persistently low ETCO2 (under 10 mmHg) despite what appears to be good CPR technique after 20 minutes most likely suggests what?
choices: A poor prognosis / low likelihood of ROSC
The patient has already achieved ROSC
The airway has been placed incorrectly regardless of technique
Compressions should be stopped and epinephrine held
questions.why: A persistently very low ETCO2 despite adequate technique correlates with poor perfusion and a lower likelihood of successful resuscitation, useful prognostic information for the team, not a sign of ROSC or a reason to stop treating.

questions.q: What is the correct energy approach for subsequent defibrillation attempts using a biphasic defibrillator when VF/pVT persists?
choices: Always use the lowest possible energy after the first shock
Use the same or a higher (escalating) energy than the previous shock, per the specific device's recommendations
Switch to monophasic settings automatically
Never exceed the first shock's energy under any circumstance
questions.why: Biphasic defibrillators vary by manufacturer, but the general approach is to use the device-specific dose or escalate energy on subsequent shocks if the rhythm persists, not to reduce power or switch technology types.

questions.q: After achieving ROSC, what is the recommended target range for oxygen saturation to avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia?
choices: 100% at all times
Below 90%
Any level is fine as long as the patient is breathing
questions.why: Post-ROSC care targets SpO2 92-98% because both hypoxia and unnecessary hyperoxia are associated with worse outcomes; deliberately targeting 100% oxygen saturation is discouraged.

questions.q: What blood pressure target is recommended immediately after ROSC to support organ perfusion?
choices: Systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg is preferred
No blood pressure target is used post-ROSC
Diastolic blood pressure under 40 mmHg is the goal
Systolic blood pressure greater than 90 mmHg (avoid hypotension)
questions.why: Maintaining SBP above 90 mmHg (often with fluids and/or vasopressors) supports brain and organ perfusion after ROSC; deliberately allowing hypotension worsens secondary injury.

questions.q: What is targeted temperature management (TTM) after ROSC in a patient who remains comatose?
choices: Maintaining a controlled constant temperature between 32-37.5°C for at least 24 hours
Actively rewarming the patient to 40°C as fast as possible
Allowing temperature to fluctuate freely with no target
Cooling the patient to 20°C for maximum neuroprotection
questions.why: Post-arrest temperature control targets a constant temperature in the 32-37.5°C range (AHA 2025; the 2020 range was 32-36°C) sustained for at least 24 hours, with fever actively prevented, to reduce secondary brain injury in comatose post-arrest patients; both active hyperthermia and extreme cooling below the target range are harmful.

questions.q: Why is hyperventilation avoided in the post-ROSC period?
choices: Hyperventilation has no known physiologic effect post-ROSC
Excessive ventilation can cause hypocapnia, which reduces cerebral blood flow and worsens neurologic outcome
Hyperventilation is preferred to maximize oxygen delivery
Hyperventilation is only a concern in pediatric patients
questions.why: Over-ventilating drives down CO2 (hypocapnia), which constricts cerebral vessels and can worsen brain injury after arrest; it is actively avoided, not preferred, regardless of patient age.

questions.q: A patient achieves ROSC but remains unresponsive. What is an appropriate next step in post-arrest care beyond airway/breathing/circulation support?
choices: Discharge planning can begin immediately
No further cardiac workup is needed once ROSC occurs
Obtain a 12-lead ECG and consider urgent coronary evaluation for a treatable cause
Withhold all further monitoring since the emergency is over
questions.why: A 12-lead ECG after ROSC screens for STEMI or another cardiac cause that may need urgent catheterization; the emergency is not over at ROSC, and ongoing monitoring/workup is essential, not optional.

questions.q: During cardiac arrest management, what is the recommended vascular access approach if IV access cannot be quickly obtained?
choices: Central line placement should always be attempted first
No medications can be given without IV access
Intramuscular injection is preferred over IO
Intraosseous (IO) access
questions.why: IO access is fast, reliable, and an accepted substitute for IV during arrest when peripheral IV access is difficult; central lines take longer to place and interrupt CPR, and IM injection doesn't achieve the rapid drug levels needed in arrest.

questions.q: What is the recommended compression technique consideration if a mechanical CPR device (like a Lucas or AutoPulse) is used?
choices: It should still deliver guideline-consistent rate/depth and minimize interruptions during application
Mechanical devices replace the need to follow rate/depth guidelines
Compressions can be paused indefinitely while the device is set up
Mechanical devices are only used for pediatric patients
questions.why: Mechanical CPR devices are tools to sustain guideline-consistent compressions, not an excuse to ignore rate/depth targets, and their application should be practiced to minimize the compression pause, not create an indefinite one.

questions.q: A rescuer wants to confirm correct endotracheal tube placement immediately after intubation during a code. What is the most reliable bedside confirmation method?
choices: Listening for breath sounds alone is fully sufficient and reliable
Waveform capnography showing a sustained CO2 waveform
X-ray must be obtained before ventilating at all
Chest rise alone confirms tracheal (not esophageal) placement
questions.why: Waveform capnography is the most reliable bedside confirmation of tracheal tube placement; breath sounds and chest rise can be misleading with esophageal intubation, and waiting for an X-ray before any ventilation would be dangerous.

questions.q: What is the correct approach to defibrillation energy selection when using a monophasic defibrillator (older technology)?
choices: 120-200 J escalating like biphasic devices
50 J fixed for every shock
360 J for all shocks
Monophasic defibrillators cannot be used for VF
questions.why: Monophasic defibrillators use a fixed maximal energy of 360 J for all shocks because they cannot deliver the more efficient biphasic waveform; the lower biphasic-style ranges don't apply to this older technology.

questions.q: A patient is defibrillated and the rhythm converts to organized complexes with a palpable pulse during the rhythm check. What should happen next?
choices: Continue CPR compressions regardless of the pulse
Give another shock immediately to be safe
Stop all monitoring since the emergency is resolved
Begin post-ROSC care: airway/oxygenation, hemodynamic support, 12-lead ECG, and identify/treat the cause
questions.why: Once a pulse and organized rhythm return, the priority shifts to post-ROSC stabilization and diagnosis, not continued compressions or an unnecessary shock; the patient still needs close monitoring, not a stop to care.

questions.q: What is the significance of a 'shockable rhythm' converting to asystole immediately after a defibrillation attempt?
choices: This can happen (post-shock asystole) and management continues with CPR and epinephrine per the non-shockable pathway
This means the defibrillator malfunctioned and must be replaced
The patient should be shocked again immediately
This always indicates death and resuscitation should stop
questions.why: Brief post-shock asystole is a recognized transitional rhythm, not a device failure or automatic indication to stop; management follows the non-shockable pathway (CPR, epinephrine) rather than another immediate shock.

questions.q: During resuscitation, what does 'team leader' responsibility primarily include?
choices: Performing all chest compressions personally throughout the code
Directing the resuscitation, assigning roles, and synthesizing information from the team to decide next steps
Only documenting the code without directing care
Standing outside the room to avoid distraction
questions.why: The team leader's core job is coordinating the resuscitation — assigning roles and integrating incoming information — rather than personally doing every hands-on task or staying detached from the room.

questions.q: A code team member believes a medication dose that was just called out was incorrect. What is the appropriate action under good team dynamics?
choices: Say nothing to avoid undermining the team leader
Give the dose they think is right without saying anything
Speak up immediately and respectfully to clarify or correct the order (constructive intervention)
Wait until after the code to mention it privately
questions.why: Constructive intervention means raising a safety concern immediately, respectfully, so it can be corrected in real time; staying silent or acting unilaterally without informing the team both risk patient harm.

questions.q: What is the recommended timing to consider terminating resuscitation efforts in an adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with no ROSC and no shockable rhythm, absent other clinical factors?
choices: Exactly 5 minutes with no ROSC
Exactly 45 minutes regardless of any other factor
Resuscitation must continue for a minimum of 2 hours in every case
This is a clinical judgment involving arrest duration, rhythm, and reversible causes — there is no single fixed time cutoff, guided by local protocol/medical direction
questions.why: Termination decisions weigh multiple factors (arrest duration, rhythm, reversible causes, EtCO2, protocol) rather than a single fixed number; picking one rigid time cutoff ignores this clinical complexity.

questions.q: A patient's rhythm shows torsades de pointes deteriorating into pulseless VT. What is the correct treatment along with standard ACLS arrest management?
choices: Consider IV magnesium sulfate in addition to defibrillation and CPR
Give calcium chloride as the first-line specific treatment
Synchronized cardioversion only, no defibrillation
Withhold epinephrine specifically for this rhythm
questions.why: Torsades responds specifically to magnesium sulfate in addition to standard defibrillation/CPR for the pulseless VT it has become; calcium isn't the specific antidote here, and once pulseless, unsynchronized defibrillation (not synchronized cardioversion) and standard epinephrine dosing still apply.

questions.q: What toxin-related reversible cause should be considered in a young patient found in cardiac arrest with a history of tricyclic antidepressant overdose and a wide QRS on the monitor?
choices: Hyperkalemia — treat with calcium chloride only
Toxins — treat with sodium bicarbonate for TCA-induced sodium channel blockade
Hypothermia — begin active rewarming
Tension pneumothorax — needle decompression
questions.why: A wide QRS with a TCA overdose history points to sodium channel blockade from the toxin, treated with sodium bicarbonate; the other options don't match this specific toxidrome and ECG clue.

questions.q: What is the role of routine sodium bicarbonate administration during a standard (non-toxin, non-hyperkalemia) cardiac arrest?
choices: It should be given to every arrest patient every 5 minutes
It replaces the need for epinephrine
It is not routinely recommended; reserved for specific situations like hyperkalemia or certain toxin overdoses
It is the first-line drug for VF
questions.why: Bicarbonate is not part of routine arrest management because it hasn't shown a broad survival benefit and can cause harm (worsening intracellular acidosis); it is reserved for specific indications like hyperkalemia or TCA toxicity, not given routinely or as an epinephrine substitute.

questions.q: What does 'return of spontaneous circulation' (ROSC) mean?
choices: The patient is fully awake and neurologically intact
The defibrillator has completed its analysis cycle
Compressions have simply reached the 2-minute mark
Sustained return of a palpable pulse and organized cardiac rhythm producing perfusion
questions.why: ROSC specifically refers to a perfusing pulse/rhythm returning, not full neurologic recovery (which may or may not follow) and unrelated to a defibrillator's analysis cycle or a compression time milestone.

questions.q: A cardiac arrest patient has a known history of severe hypothermia (core temp 28°C) from cold water immersion. How does this affect defibrillation attempts for VF?
choices: Defibrillation is still attempted, though the rhythm may be refractory until rewarming occurs; continue CPR and rewarming efforts
Defibrillation should never be attempted below 30°C
No CPR should be performed until the patient is fully rewarmed
Epinephrine should be given at double the normal dose
questions.why: Severe hypothermia can make VF refractory to shocks and drugs, but defibrillation is still attempted (often limited to one attempt until rewarming per some protocols) alongside continued CPR and active rewarming, not withheld or doubled in dosing.

questions.q: What is the correct interpretation of 'pulseless VT' on a monitor?
choices: A narrow-complex rhythm always associated with a strong pulse
An organized wide-complex tachycardia rhythm in a patient with no palpable pulse — treated as a shockable rhythm like VF
A rhythm that should be treated with synchronized cardioversion only
A rhythm managed the same as asystole
questions.why: Pulseless VT is wide-complex and organized-looking but produces no effective pulse, so it is treated on the shockable (VF) pathway with immediate defibrillation, not synchronized cardioversion (used for perfusing tachycardias) or the non-shockable PEA/asystole pathway.

questions.q: During a resuscitation, who is typically responsible for tracking time, medications given, and shocks delivered?
choices: The compressor, in addition to giving compressions
No one; time tracking is not necessary during a code
A designated recorder/timer role on the team
The patient's family member present in the room
questions.why: A dedicated recorder/timer role keeps track of interventions and timing so the team leader can make decisions without needing to also track the clock; asking the compressor to multitask or omitting this role entirely reduces situational awareness.

questions.q: What defines 'refractory VF' in the context of ongoing resuscitation?
choices: VF that responds immediately to the first shock
Any VF lasting longer than 30 seconds
VF that occurs only in patients over age 65
VF that persists despite appropriate CPR, defibrillation attempts, and antiarrhythmic medications
questions.why: Refractory VF specifically means the shockable rhythm is not converting despite guideline-directed treatment (shocks, CPR, drugs); a rhythm converting on the first shock or an arbitrary time/age cutoff doesn't define this term.

questions.q: A cardiac arrest patient has known end-stage renal disease and missed dialysis for a week, with arrest occurring shortly after IV potassium chloride was mistakenly given. Which H is most directly implicated?
choices: Hyperkalemia
Hypovolemia
Hydrogen ion (acidosis) alone
Hypothermia
questions.why: Missed dialysis plus an accidental potassium chloride dose points directly to hyperkalemia as the precipitant, treated urgently with calcium, insulin/glucose, and bicarbonate; the other H's don't connect to this specific history.

questions.q: What should be reassessed at every 2-minute rhythm/pulse check during a resuscitation?
choices: Only the patient's temperature
The cardiac rhythm, whether a pulse is present, and the ongoing quality of CPR
Only whether family should be allowed in the room
Only the battery level of the defibrillator
questions.why: Rhythm checks are the structured point to reassess the actual clinical picture — rhythm, pulse, and CPR quality — driving the next treatment decision; the other items are not the purpose of this periodic check.

questions.q: What is a key documentation element that should be captured for every defibrillation attempt during a code?
choices: Only the total number of shocks given, with no other detail
The defibrillator serial number only
Time of shock, energy delivered, and the rhythm before and after the shock
Nothing needs to be recorded until after the code ends
questions.why: Detailed real-time documentation (time, energy, pre/post rhythm) supports clinical decision-making during the code and accurate post-event review; recording only a shock count or nothing at all loses information needed for the case.

questions.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has a large recent GI bleed noted in their chart. Which H is most relevant to address as a reversible cause?
choices: Hypothermia
Tension pneumothorax
Toxins
Hypovolemia
questions.why: Significant blood loss from a GI bleed causes hypovolemia, addressed with rapid IV fluids and blood products during the arrest; the other options have no direct link to this history.

questions.q: What is the appropriate action if, during CPR, a rescuer suspects the endotracheal tube has become dislodged (rising resistance, no chest rise, no capnography waveform)?
choices: Immediately reassess airway placement and correct or replace the tube as needed
Ignore it since compressions are the priority and airway can wait indefinitely
Give a double dose of epinephrine to compensate
Assume it is fine since capnography can be unreliable
questions.why: Loss of chest rise and capnography waveform are strong signs of a dislodged or malpositioned tube, which must be addressed promptly since ventilation is compromised; more epinephrine does not fix an airway problem, and dismissing clear capnography loss risks prolonged hypoxia.

questions.q: A patient has a heart rate of 38/min, is hypotensive, and is confused. What is this classified as?
choices: Symptomatic (unstable) bradycardia requiring immediate treatment
Stable bradycardia that only needs observation
A shockable rhythm requiring defibrillation
Normal sinus bradycardia seen in athletes
questions.why: Hypotension and altered mental status with a slow rate define symptomatic bradycardia needing active treatment; it is not a shockable rhythm, and athletic bradycardia is asymptomatic by definition, unlike this presentation.

questions.q: What is the first-line drug and dose for symptomatic bradycardia in the ACLS algorithm?
choices: Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Atropine 1 mg IV, may repeat every 3-5 minutes
Adenosine 6 mg IV rapid push
Epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes as first-line
questions.why: Atropine 1 mg IV (repeatable) is first-line for symptomatic bradycardia; amiodarone and adenosine are tachycardia/arrest drugs, and epinephrine is used as a second-line infusion if atropine fails, not first.

questions.q: Atropine fails to improve a symptomatic bradycardic patient. What are appropriate next steps?
choices: A second dose of adenosine 12 mg IV
Immediate defibrillation
Transcutaneous pacing and/or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Synchronized cardioversion at 50 J
questions.why: When atropine fails, transcutaneous pacing or a chronotropic infusion (dopamine or epinephrine) is the next step; adenosine and cardioversion/defibrillation are not indicated for a slow, non-tachycardic rhythm.

questions.q: What is a key nursing/paramedic consideration when starting transcutaneous pacing on an awake, symptomatic bradycardic patient?
choices: No pain management is ever needed for pacing
Pacing must always be done without the patient's knowledge
Pacing pads should never be used on a conscious patient
Provide analgesia/sedation, since pacing is painful
questions.why: Transcutaneous pacing causes significant discomfort from skeletal muscle contraction, so analgesia/sedation is given when the patient is awake enough to feel it; conscious patients can and do receive pacing when indicated, just with comfort measures.

questions.q: A patient with symptomatic bradycardia after a recent heart transplant does not respond well to atropine. Why might this occur?
choices: A transplanted heart is denervated, so atropine (which works via the vagus nerve) is often ineffective
Atropine is contraindicated in all cardiac patients
Transplant patients cannot receive any bradycardia treatment
Atropine only works in patients over age 65
questions.why: Because a transplanted heart lacks vagal innervation, atropine's vagolytic mechanism doesn't work well, so pacing or catecholamine infusions are typically needed instead; atropine isn't broadly contraindicated in cardiac patients generally.

questions.q: A stable patient has a narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 180/min with no hypotension, chest pain, or altered mental status. What is an appropriate first-line treatment attempt?
choices: Immediate synchronized cardioversion
Vagal maneuvers, followed by adenosine if unsuccessful
Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation
IV amiodarone as the first step
questions.why: Stable narrow-complex SVT is first managed with vagal maneuvers, then adenosine if those fail; cardioversion (synchronized) and amiodarone are reserved for when adenosine/vagal maneuvers don't work or the patient becomes unstable, and defibrillation is never appropriate for a rhythm with a pulse.

questions.q: What is the correct first adenosine dose for stable regular narrow-complex SVT?
choices: 12 mg as the first dose
1 mg as the first dose
6 mg rapid IV push, followed by a rapid saline flush
6 mg given slowly over 5 minutes
questions.why: 6 mg rapid IV push (immediately flushed) is the correct first adenosine dose; 12 mg is the second/third dose if needed, and adenosine's very short half-life means it must be pushed rapidly, not given slowly.

questions.q: If the first adenosine dose does not convert a stable SVT, what is the next dose?
choices: 6 mg repeated, identical to the first dose
3 mg rapid IV push
18 mg rapid IV push
12 mg rapid IV push
questions.why: The standard escalation is 6 mg then 12 mg (sometimes a second 12 mg dose); halving to 3 mg or jumping to 18 mg are not the guideline-based doses.

questions.q: A patient with a narrow-complex tachycardia at 170/min is hypotensive, diaphoretic, and has altered mental status. What is the appropriate treatment?
choices: Immediate synchronized cardioversion
Vagal maneuvers only, then reassess in 10 minutes
Oral beta-blocker therapy
Unsynchronized defibrillation
questions.why: Hypotension, diaphoresis, and altered mental status indicate unstable tachycardia requiring immediate synchronized cardioversion, not a slower vagal-maneuver trial, oral medication, or unsynchronized defibrillation (which is for pulseless/chaotic rhythms, not a perfusing tachycardia).

questions.q: What is the key difference between synchronized cardioversion and defibrillation?
choices: They are identical procedures with different names
Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to the QRS complex to avoid the T wave, defibrillation does not
Defibrillation is only used for bradycardia
Synchronized cardioversion is used only in pulseless patients
questions.why: Synchronization avoids delivering the shock during the vulnerable T wave, which could induce VF; defibrillation for a pulseless, chaotic rhythm has no organized QRS to sync to, so it is delivered immediately without timing, and neither is used for bradycardia.

questions.q: Why is timing the shock to the QRS complex important during synchronized cardioversion?
choices: It has no real clinical importance, just a formality
It ensures the patient feels no pain
Shocking during the T wave (R-on-T phenomenon) can induce ventricular fibrillation
It is only relevant for pediatric patients
questions.why: The R-on-T phenomenon — shocking during the heart's vulnerable repolarization period — can precipitate VF, which is exactly why synchronization is built into the cardioversion process; it does not affect pain and applies to adults as well as children.

questions.q: A wide-complex tachycardia patient is stable with a regular rhythm. What is an appropriate treatment consideration in addition to expert consultation?
choices: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation regardless of pulse
High-dose atropine as first-line
Vagal maneuvers as the definitive treatment
Antiarrhythmic infusion (e.g., procainamide or amiodarone) or elective cardioversion
questions.why: Stable regular wide-complex tachycardia may be treated with an antiarrhythmic infusion or cardioversion; unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless patients, atropine treats bradycardia not tachycardia, and vagal maneuvers alone are not definitive for a wide-complex rhythm.

questions.q: An unstable wide-complex tachycardia patient with a pulse needs treatment. What is indicated?
choices: Synchronized cardioversion
Unsynchronized defibrillation
IV atropine 1 mg
Oral antiarrhythmic loading dose
questions.why: An unstable but pulsed wide-complex tachycardia is treated with synchronized cardioversion; unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms, atropine treats slow rates not fast ones, and oral dosing is far too slow for an unstable patient.

questions.q: A patient presents with crushing substernal chest pain, diaphoresis, and ST elevation on the monitor. What is the recommended door-to-balloon time goal for primary PCI?
choices: Less than 6 hours
Less than 90 minutes
Less than 24 hours
There is no time goal for PCI
questions.why: The door-to-balloon goal for STEMI is under 90 minutes because 'time is muscle' — myocardial damage accumulates the longer the artery stays occluded; hours-long goals would allow far more infarction to occur.

questions.q: What is the recommended initial aspirin dose for a suspected acute coronary syndrome patient without contraindications?
choices: 81 mg, swallowed whole
650 mg, chewed
162-325 mg, chewed
Aspirin is not given in suspected ACS
questions.why: A chewed non-enteric dose of 162-325 mg is recommended because chewing speeds absorption for faster antiplatelet effect; the low-dose 81 mg maintenance tablet and swallowing whole both delay onset compared to chewing the correct dose.

questions.q: A chest pain patient's 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which coronary territory is most likely involved?
choices: Anterior wall (LAD territory)
Lateral wall (circumflex territory) exclusively
This pattern indicates a pulmonary embolism, not MI
Inferior wall (right coronary artery territory in most patients)
questions.why: II, III, and aVF are the inferior leads, typically supplied by the right coronary artery; anterior changes would appear in V1-V4, and this specific inferior pattern is not a PE finding.

questions.q: Why should nitroglycerin be used cautiously or avoided in a suspected ACS patient who reports recent use of a phosphodiesterase inhibitor (e.g., sildenafil) within 24-48 hours?
choices: The combination can cause severe, refractory hypotension
It has no interaction and can be given freely
It will cause immediate hypertension instead
It will cause a false-positive troponin
questions.why: Both nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors cause vasodilation, and combined they can cause profound, hard-to-reverse hypotension; the interaction causes low blood pressure, not high, and has nothing to do with troponin results.

questions.q: What is the target door-to-CT time for a suspected acute ischemic stroke patient?
choices: Within 3 hours of arrival
Within 25 minutes of arrival
Within 24 hours of arrival
CT is not time-sensitive for stroke
questions.why: Rapid CT imaging (goal under 25 minutes) is needed to quickly distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke and determine tPA eligibility, since treatment is highly time-sensitive; hours-long windows would delay a time-critical decision.

questions.q: What is the standard tPA (alteplase) treatment window from last known well for eligible ischemic stroke patients?
choices: Within 24 hours for all patients, no exceptions
Within 15 minutes only
Within 3 hours, extendable to 4.5 hours for select patients
There is no time window; tPA can be given anytime
questions.why: The classic tPA window is 3 hours, extended to 4.5 hours for certain eligible patients; a blanket 24-hour window or unlimited window is inaccurate, and 15 minutes is far too short to realistically administer tPA.

questions.q: What is the recommended door-to-needle time goal for administering tPA in an eligible stroke patient?
choices: Within 6 hours of arrival
Within 10 minutes of arrival
There is no specific door-to-needle goal
Within 60 minutes of arrival
questions.why: The door-to-needle goal of under 60 minutes balances thoroughness (ruling out hemorrhage, checking eligibility) with the urgency of 'time is brain'; 10 minutes is unrealistically fast for the required workup, and 6 hours would squander much of the treatment window.

questions.q: What does the 'FAST' stroke recognition tool stand for?
choices: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call for help
Fever, Altered mental status, Seizure, Tachycardia
Focused Assessment for Stroke Treatment
Fluids, Airway, Suction, Transport
questions.why: FAST is the public/prehospital recognition tool for stroke symptoms and the urgency of getting care fast; the distractors are unrelated acronyms or don't match the actual established meaning of FAST.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS)?
choices: To measure blood glucose in a stroke patient
To objectively quantify stroke severity and guide treatment decisions
To calculate the patient's door-to-balloon time
To determine cardiac arrest reversibility
questions.why: NIHSS is a standardized neurologic exam score that quantifies deficit severity and helps guide treatment and prognosis discussions; it has nothing to do with glucose, cardiac door-to-balloon metrics, or arrest reversibility.

questions.q: A stroke patient is being considered for tPA. What blood pressure threshold generally must be met before administration?
choices: Below 220/120 mmHg
Above 200/110 mmHg
Generally below 185/110 mmHg
Blood pressure is not a consideration for tPA eligibility
questions.why: Blood pressure must generally be brought below 185/110 mmHg before tPA to reduce hemorrhagic risk; 220/120 is too high a threshold to allow safely, and BP is very much a relevant eligibility factor, not irrelevant.

questions.q: A patient with acute ischemic stroke symptoms has a 'last known well' time of 5.5 hours ago and no large vessel occlusion identified for thrombectomy. What is the most appropriate statement about tPA?
choices: tPA should be given regardless of time elapsed
tPA is always safe up to 24 hours
The time window does not apply if symptoms are severe
tPA is generally no longer indicated since the time window (up to 4.5 hours) has passed
questions.why: Once past the extended 4.5-hour window, tPA's bleeding risk generally outweighs benefit, so it is not given outside strict extended-window criteria; symptom severity alone does not override the established time cutoff.

questions.q: What does 'time is muscle' refer to in the context of ACS management?
choices: The longer a coronary artery stays occluded, the more myocardium is permanently damaged
It refers to how fast CPR compressions should be given
It means muscle relaxants should be given quickly
It refers to how fast a patient should be moved to a stretcher
questions.why: 'Time is muscle' captures why rapid reperfusion (PCI or fibrinolysis) matters in ACS — ongoing occlusion kills more heart muscle each minute; it is unrelated to CPR rate, muscle relaxants, or patient transport logistics.

questions.q: A patient with suspected ACS reports allergy to aspirin with a history of true anaphylaxis. What is the appropriate action regarding aspirin?
choices: Give aspirin anyway since ACS always overrides allergy history
Withhold aspirin and consider an alternative antiplatelet per protocol/physician guidance
Double the aspirin dose to compensate
No antiplatelet therapy of any kind should be used
questions.why: A true anaphylactic allergy is a real contraindication, so aspirin is withheld and an alternative considered; overriding a genuine anaphylaxis history or doubling the dose risks a severe allergic reaction, and other antiplatelet options can still be considered.

questions.q: Why might morphine be used cautiously (not as a routine first step) in ACS chest pain management today, compared to older practice?
choices: Morphine is now considered completely contraindicated in all ACS
Morphine improves reperfusion time when given first
Studies suggest morphine may mask ongoing ischemic symptoms and has been associated with worse outcomes in some ACS patients
Morphine has no known effect on ACS outcomes
questions.why: Evidence linking morphine to potentially masking symptoms and worse outcomes has shifted it from a routine first-line comfort measure to a more selective use (for refractory pain after nitrates); it isn't absolutely contraindicated, but it's also not benefit-neutral or reperfusion-enhancing.

questions.q: A hemorrhagic stroke is identified on initial CT instead of ischemic stroke. What is the correct action regarding tPA?
choices: tPA should be given at a reduced dose
tPA timing simply needs to be delayed by 1 hour
There is no difference in treatment between hemorrhagic and ischemic stroke
tPA is contraindicated and must not be given
questions.why: tPA is a thrombolytic and would worsen an active bleed, making hemorrhagic stroke an absolute contraindication, not something managed with a reduced dose or short delay; the two stroke types require fundamentally different treatment approaches.

questions.q: What is the correct initial management priority for a patient presenting with signs of acute stroke, before any imaging?
choices: Rapid assessment of airway/breathing/circulation, blood glucose check, and determining last known well time
Immediate tPA administration without any assessment
Immediate intubation of every stroke patient
Cardiac catheterization before any neuro assessment
questions.why: Basic ABCs, a glucose check (to rule out hypoglycemia mimicking stroke), and establishing last known well time are essential before any stroke-specific treatment; tPA is never given without an assessment/CT first, and neither intubation nor cath is a default step.

questions.q: A stable patient has irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. What is a reasonable initial approach if the patient remains stable?
choices: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation
Rate control (e.g., beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker) rather than immediate cardioversion
Adenosine as definitive treatment
Immediate synchronized cardioversion regardless of stability
questions.why: Stable rapid atrial fibrillation is typically managed with rate control medications first; adenosine is not a definitive treatment for AFib (it's for reentrant SVT), defibrillation is for pulseless patients, and cardioversion is reserved for unstable patients or specific elective circumstances.

questions.q: What historical/clinical factor is important to check before elective or urgent cardioversion of atrial fibrillation (beyond the emergent unstable scenario)?
choices: The patient's shoe size and recent travel history
Whether the patient prefers oral or IV medications
Duration of the arrhythmia and stroke/clot risk (e.g., need for anticoagulation or TEE to rule out atrial thrombus)
The color of the cardiac monitor tracing
questions.why: AFib lasting more than about 48 hours carries meaningful risk of atrial thrombus that could embolize with cardioversion, so duration and anticoagulation status matter; the other listed factors have no bearing on cardioversion safety.

questions.q: A patient with bradycardia has a narrow-complex rhythm at 45/min but is completely asymptomatic (no hypotension, chest pain, or altered mental status). What is the appropriate management?
choices: Give atropine 1 mg IV immediately regardless of symptoms
Begin transcutaneous pacing immediately
Perform synchronized cardioversion
Monitor closely without immediate pharmacologic or electrical treatment
questions.why: Asymptomatic bradycardia (like in a fit athlete) generally requires only observation, since treatment is driven by symptoms, not the number alone; atropine, pacing, and cardioversion are all interventions reserved for symptomatic or unstable presentations.

questions.q: What ECG finding is most concerning for a posterior wall MI that can be easily missed on a standard 12-lead?
choices: ST depression and tall R waves in leads V1-V2 (a 'mirror image' of posterior elevation)
ST elevation in aVR only, always benign
A completely normal-appearing ECG rules out any MI
Isolated T-wave flattening in lead III
questions.why: Posterior MI shows as reciprocal ST depression and tall R waves anteriorly (V1-V2) since standard leads don't directly view the posterior wall; a normal-appearing ECG does not reliably rule out MI, and isolated lead III T-wave flattening is a nonspecific, less concerning finding.

questions.q: What is an appropriate action for a stable patient with new-onset atrial fibrillation and a rapid ventricular rate who also has signs of decompensated heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension)?
choices: Give a large IV fluid bolus first regardless of the pulmonary edema
Treat as unstable and proceed to synchronized cardioversion
Use adenosine as definitive treatment
Continue rate-control medications only, no escalation
questions.why: Hypotension and pulmonary edema from the arrhythmia indicate hemodynamic instability, which shifts management to synchronized cardioversion; a fluid bolus would worsen pulmonary edema, adenosine isn't definitive for AFib, and rate control alone is inadequate for an unstable patient.

questions.q: What does 'reperfusion therapy' refer to broadly in ACS management?
choices: Giving supplemental oxygen to all chest pain patients regardless of saturation
Administering IV fluids to raise blood pressure
Restoring blood flow through the blocked coronary artery, via PCI or fibrinolytics
Performing chest compressions during a STEMI
questions.why: Reperfusion therapy specifically means mechanically (PCI) or pharmacologically (fibrinolytics) reopening the blocked artery; routine oxygen for a normally saturated patient, fluids, and compressions are separate interventions, not reperfusion itself.

questions.q: In a rural setting without timely access to PCI for a STEMI patient, what alternative treatment should be considered?
choices: No treatment is available outside of PCI centers
Synchronized cardioversion as a substitute for PCI
Withhold all treatment until transfer, regardless of time
Fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) therapy
questions.why: When PCI cannot be delivered within the guideline time window, fibrinolytic therapy is the recommended alternative reperfusion strategy; cardioversion treats arrhythmias, not coronary occlusion, and withholding treatment during a long transfer would allow unnecessary myocardial damage.

questions.q: A patient receiving a dopamine infusion for symptomatic bradycardia after failed atropine develops worsening tachyarrhythmia. What is an appropriate response?
choices: Titrate down or stop the infusion and reassess the rhythm and hemodynamics
Increase the dopamine dose to compensate
Switch immediately to high-dose epinephrine at cardiac arrest doses
Ignore the new arrhythmia since bradycardia was the primary problem
questions.why: Catecholamine infusions like dopamine can themselves provoke tachyarrhythmias, so the appropriate response is to reduce/stop and reassess rather than push the dose higher or ignore a new problem; jumping to arrest-dose epinephrine is not appropriate for a patient who has a pulse and isn't in arrest.

questions.q: What is a key reason vagal maneuvers (like the modified Valsalva) are tried before adenosine in stable SVT?
choices: They are more effective than adenosine in every case
They are noninvasive, low-risk, and can terminate the reentrant circuit without medication
They have significant risk and should only be a last resort
They only work in patients over age 70
questions.why: Vagal maneuvers carry very low risk and can be effective for reentrant SVT, making them a sensible first try before medication; they are not universally more effective than adenosine, are lower risk (not higher), and are not age-restricted in that way.

questions.q: A patient has stable monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia. Expert consultation is recommended. What is an important reason for this recommendation?
choices: Expert consultation is only a formality with no real clinical reason
Wide-complex tachycardia is always benign and treatment doesn't matter
Wide-complex tachycardia can be VT or SVT with aberrancy, and treatment differs; misdiagnosis (e.g., giving verapamil for VT) can be harmful
There is no risk in treating any wide-complex tachycardia the same way
questions.why: Distinguishing VT from SVT with aberrant conduction matters because some treatments (like certain calcium channel blockers) can cause hemodynamic collapse if the rhythm is actually VT; this is a genuine clinical safety issue, not a formality, and the two causes are not treated identically.

questions.q: What is the significance of new left bundle branch block (LBBB) in a patient with chest pain?
choices: LBBB is always a benign, chronic finding requiring no action
LBBB indicates the patient needs immediate synchronized cardioversion
LBBB rules out any cardiac cause of the chest pain
New LBBB with a suggestive clinical picture can indicate an evolving MI and may warrant treatment as a STEMI-equivalent
questions.why: A new LBBB in the setting of chest pain is treated with high suspicion for MI since it can obscure typical ST-elevation criteria; it does not rule out cardiac cause, and cardioversion is not the appropriate response to a conduction abnormality without an arrhythmia to treat.

questions.q: What is an important consideration when giving nitroglycerin to a chest pain patient regarding blood pressure?
