choices: Check blood pressure before and after doses, since nitroglycerin can cause hypotension
Blood pressure does not need to be checked with nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin always raises blood pressure significantly
Nitroglycerin has no cardiovascular effects
questions.why: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator that can drop blood pressure, sometimes significantly, so it must be monitored before and after each dose; it lowers (not raises) blood pressure and clearly does have cardiovascular effects.

questions.q: A patient with acute stroke symptoms is found to have a blood glucose of 45 mg/dL. What is the appropriate initial action?
choices: Proceed directly to tPA administration without checking further
Treat the hypoglycemia, since it can mimic stroke symptoms and may resolve with glucose correction
Ignore the glucose value and focus only on the NIHSS score
Assume this confirms a hemorrhagic stroke
questions.why: Hypoglycemia is a well-known stroke mimic, and correcting it may resolve the neurologic symptoms entirely, so it must be treated and reassessed before proceeding with stroke-specific therapy; the glucose value doesn't confirm a hemorrhage and shouldn't be ignored.

questions.q: Why is obtaining IV access and drawing labs generally done in parallel with, not before, getting the stroke patient to CT?
choices: Labs are more important than imaging for treatment decisions
IV access must always be established before any imaging occurs
CT imaging to rule out hemorrhage is extremely time-sensitive and should not be delayed by other tasks that can happen simultaneously
CT imaging can safely wait until all labs return
questions.why: Because tPA eligibility is so time-sensitive, teams work in parallel — moving to CT quickly while IV access/labs are obtained alongside — rather than sequencing tasks that would waste minutes; neither IV access nor labs should hold up the CT.

questions.q: What is 'closed-loop communication' in a resuscitation team?
choices: The sender gives an order, the receiver repeats it back, and the sender confirms it was understood correctly
Only the team leader is allowed to speak during the code
Communication that happens only through written notes
Team members work silently to avoid distracting the leader
questions.why: Closed-loop communication (order, read-back, confirmation) prevents mishearing critical instructions like drug doses; silence or written-only notes are far too slow and error-prone during a time-critical resuscitation.

questions.q: What does 'knowing your limitations' mean as a team dynamics principle in ACLS?
choices: Refusing to perform any task you have not done before, even under supervision
Recognizing when a task is beyond your training or capacity and asking for help or reassignment
Never asking questions during a code to appear confident
Always deferring every decision to the most senior person present
questions.why: Knowing your limitations means speaking up for help or clarification when a task exceeds your skill or capacity, which protects the patient; refusing all new tasks or silently deferring everything undermines effective teamwork just as much as overreaching.

questions.q: What is meant by 'constructive intervention' during a code?
choices: Taking over the resuscitation without informing anyone
Criticizing team members after the code has ended only
Respectfully speaking up in real time to correct an error or suggest a better course of action
Avoiding any comment on another team member's actions
questions.why: Constructive intervention is timely, respectful real-time correction — the opposite of silent avoidance or unilateral takeover, both of which either let errors persist or bypass the team leader's coordination.

questions.q: Why does the ACLS team dynamics model emphasize clear roles for each team member?
choices: Clear roles are mainly for legal documentation, not patient care
Roles do not actually matter as long as everyone helps generally
Having defined roles slows the team down
Clear roles reduce duplicated or missed tasks and improve efficiency during a high-stress resuscitation
questions.why: Assigned roles (compressor, airway, medications, recorder, leader) prevent both gaps and duplication of effort under stress, directly improving the resuscitation's efficiency — not merely paperwork, and clearly not something that slows the team.

questions.q: During a code, the team leader assigns a task to a specific team member by name and makes eye contact. Why is this preferred over a general announcement to the room?
choices: Directed communication to a named individual ensures someone specific takes ownership of the task
It has no advantage over a general announcement
It is only useful for very small teams of two people
General announcements are always clearer than direct requests
questions.why: A task announced to the whole room risks the 'bystander effect' where everyone assumes someone else will do it; naming a specific person with eye contact ensures clear ownership, a documented advantage regardless of team size.

questions.q: What is 'knowledge sharing' as a team dynamics element in resuscitation?
choices: Only the team leader is permitted to know clinical information
Team members openly voicing relevant information or ideas, even if it means questioning the current plan
Sharing knowledge is limited to after-action debriefs
Team members should keep observations to themselves unless directly asked
questions.why: Knowledge sharing means any team member can offer relevant information proactively during the event, not just the leader holding all information or team members staying silent unless asked; that openness catches things the leader alone might miss.

questions.q: What is a 'debriefing' after a resuscitation attempt primarily used for?
choices: Assigning blame to a specific team member for the outcome
Filling out billing paperwork only
Reviewing what went well and what could improve, to strengthen future team performance
Determining who gets to lead the next code
questions.why: Debriefing is a structured, blame-free review of performance to identify improvements for next time; it is not about punishing an individual, billing, or deciding future leadership assignments.

questions.q: What is an example of 'mutual respect' in team dynamics during a resuscitation?
choices: Only respecting the opinions of physicians on the team
Raising your voice is an acceptable way to convey urgency at all times
Ignoring input from newer or less experienced team members
Communicating calmly and professionally with team members regardless of their role or experience level
questions.why: Mutual respect means valuing input across all roles and experience levels with calm professional communication; dismissing junior members or normalizing yelling both erode the psychological safety needed for people to speak up.

questions.q: A team member is unsure how to correctly operate a piece of equipment during a code. What is the appropriate action per team dynamics principles?
choices: Ask for help or hand off the task to someone who knows how to use it
Attempt it anyway without asking, to avoid looking inexperienced
Pretend the equipment is broken to avoid the task
Wait silently until someone else notices the problem
questions.why: Asking for help or reassigning the task is the 'know your limitations' principle in action, keeping the patient safe; struggling silently, faking a malfunction, or hoping someone notices all risk delayed or incorrect care.

questions.q: What is the purpose of assigning a dedicated recorder during a resuscitation?
choices: To take photographs of the resuscitation for social media
To accurately track times, medications, interventions, and rhythm changes for real-time reference and later review
To manage family communication exclusively
To perform compressions when the primary compressor tires
questions.why: The recorder's job is accurate real-time documentation the team leader can reference (e.g., 'when is the next epi due?'), which also supports post-event review; it has nothing to do with photography, is not the designated family liaison role, and is a separate role from compressions.

questions.q: How should a team leader ideally communicate an order for a medication during a code?
choices: Use vague language like 'give the usual dose' to save time
Only write the order on paper without saying it aloud
State the drug name, dose, and route clearly and directly to a specific team member
Assume the team already knows what to give without stating it
questions.why: Explicit, specific verbal orders (drug, dose, route) directed at a person prevent dosing errors; vague phrasing, silent written-only orders, or assuming shared knowledge all increase the risk of a mistake during a fast-moving code.

questions.q: What should happen if two team members give conflicting information about the patient's rhythm during a code?
choices: Proceed with whichever team member spoke first, regardless of accuracy
Ignore both reports and wait for the next scheduled rhythm check
Let family members present decide which report to trust
Clarify immediately, ideally by re-checking the monitor together, before proceeding with treatment
questions.why: Conflicting critical information must be resolved immediately since treatment (like a shock) depends on the rhythm being correct; picking based on who spoke first, waiting arbitrarily, or involving family in a clinical decision are all inappropriate ways to resolve this.

questions.q: Why is it important for the team leader to periodically summarize the situation out loud during a prolonged resuscitation?
choices: It keeps the whole team oriented to the current status, what has been done, and what's next
It is required only for legal documentation purposes
It is unnecessary if the code is going well
Summaries should only occur at the very end of the code
questions.why: Periodic summarizing (a core team dynamics behavior) keeps every team member's mental model synchronized on status and next steps, useful regardless of how smoothly the code seems to be going, not just for paperwork or reserved for the end.

questions.q: A new, less experienced team member is asked to perform chest compressions during a code. What is the appropriate approach if they feel unsure about their technique?
choices: Continue without saying anything to avoid seeming incompetent
Voice the uncertainty and ask for feedback or a demonstration from a more experienced team member
Refuse to perform compressions entirely without explanation
Stop the code to leave the room and look up a reference video
questions.why: Speaking up for real-time feedback keeps compression quality high while respecting the 'know your limitations' principle; hiding uncertainty, refusing without explanation, or stopping the whole code to self-study are all worse for the patient in the moment.

questions.q: What best describes the team leader's responsibility regarding assigning the defibrillator/monitor role?
choices: Any bystander in the room can be assigned this role without training
The team leader must always personally operate the defibrillator
Assign it to a team member trained in rhythm recognition and safe shock delivery, and confirm they understand the role
This role does not need to be assigned; anyone can grab it
questions.why: Defibrillation requires specific training for accurate rhythm interpretation and safe shock delivery, so this role goes to a qualified person with confirmed understanding, not an untrained bystander, an undefined 'anyone,' or a rule that forces the leader to always do it personally.

questions.q: During a resuscitation, a family member is present and distressed in the room. What is an appropriate team dynamics consideration?
choices: Family presence should always be denied during any resuscitation
No one should ever speak to the family during the event
The team leader should stop directing care to personally comfort the family
Assign a team member (if staffing allows) to support and communicate with the family without disrupting the resuscitation
questions.why: Family presence, where supported by protocol, is managed by assigning a support person so clinical roles stay intact; blanket denial, total silence toward family, or having the leader abandon direction of care are all poor approaches to this real scenario.

questions.q: What is an appropriate way for a team member to express disagreement with the team leader's chosen treatment plan during a code?
choices: State the concern clearly and offer a rationale or alternative in real time, respecting the leader's final call
Comply outwardly but intentionally perform the task incorrectly
Refuse to participate in the code until the plan changes
Wait until after the resuscitation is completely over to mention it
questions.why: Voicing a respectful, real-time concern lets the team leader weigh new information while keeping the team functional; passive resistance, refusing to help, or delaying feedback until after the event are all worse for patient safety in the moment.

questions.q: What is the value of a structured post-event debrief format (such as discussing what went well, what was challenging, and what to change)?
choices: It replaces the need for any documentation of the code
It creates a consistent, constructive process for improving future team performance rather than an unstructured venting session
It is only useful for events with a poor outcome
It should focus solely on criticizing the team leader
questions.why: A structured format (well/challenging/change) keeps debriefs constructive and consistent for both good and bad outcomes; it doesn't replace clinical documentation and should never be a one-sided leader-blaming session.

questions.q: Why is it considered good practice for the team leader to remain hands-off from direct tasks like compressions when enough staff are available?
choices: Team leaders are not permitted to ever touch the patient
It has no bearing on the quality of leadership during a code
It allows the leader to maintain situational awareness of the whole resuscitation rather than being absorbed in one task
Team leaders should always perform every task personally to set an example
questions.why: Staying hands-off (when staffing allows) lets the leader watch the whole picture — timing, rhythm changes, team performance — rather than tunnel-visioning on one task; this is a practical leadership choice, not an absolute rule against ever touching the patient nor a mandate to do everything personally.
